iterations.explanation: No previous user feedback was provided. Data Storage and Access Pattern captures organization and retrieval; Data and Feature Preparation Workflow captures transformation; Model Search and Training Strategy captures model construction; Workflow Composition and Orchestration captures execution structure; ML Verification and Testing Strategy captures assurance; Model Serving Architecture captures inference exposure; Deployment and Lifecycle Automation captures release evolution; Production Operations and Governance captures runtime control. These axes are orthogonal because they answer different architectural questions across the ML workflow. Values preserve accepted, rejected, and outcome statuses, including near-duplicates when their statuses differ, such as continuous monitoring versus model degradation and coordinated versus duplicated pipelines. Relations express workflow preconditions, operational consequences, and constraints rather than incidental co-occurrence.

clusters.name: Data Storage and Access Pattern
clusters.description: Documents vary in how ML data is organized, stored, and accessed before preparation, distinct from transformations applied to the data.

relations.rationale: The storage and access arrangement determines which data can be supplied to preparation and feature-engineering workflows.

values.label: Centralized consistently structured storage
values.description: Data is collected in a convenient, consistently structured location for reliable ML use.

values.label: Analyst-controlled query extraction
values.description: Analysts independently retrieve modeling data through queries rather than relying entirely on a centralized data-science team.

values.label: Scattered multi-language asset storage
values.description: Data-science assets are distributed across locations, environments, and programming languages without controlled organization.

clusters.name: Data and Feature Preparation Workflow
clusters.description: Documents vary in how raw data is transformed, analyzed, and converted into model-ready features, rather than how it is stored.

relations.rationale: Prepared data and engineered features are inputs to model-training and model-search decisions.
The preparation workflow determines the stages and dependencies that orchestration must execute.

values.label: Dedicated feature-engineering pipeline
values.description: A reusable pipeline selects, transforms, combines, and prepares raw data for algorithmic modeling.

values.label: Analyst-managed preprocessing
values.description: Analysts use AutoML tooling to preprocess extracted data without requiring the full data-science team.

values.label: Automated data and feature analysis
values.description: The workflow automatically summarizes data and analyzes feature behavior before or alongside training.

values.label: Duplicated independently recreated pipelines
values.description: Separate practitioners recreate ETL, data-quality, and feature-engineering pipelines for the same source.

clusters.name: Model Search and Training Strategy
clusters.description: Documents vary in how algorithms, hyperparameters, execution order, and reproducibility are selected and controlled during model construction.

relations.rationale: Training choices produce the candidate models that verification and quality testing must assess.
Training parallelism and execution requirements constrain the orchestration and compute workflow.

values.label: AutoML multi-algorithm search
values.description: AutoML evaluates multiple algorithm types and candidate models rather than relying on one manually selected algorithm.

values.label: Automated concurrent hyperparameter tuning
values.description: Multiple model types or training configurations are tuned concurrently to reduce manual effort and search time.

values.label: Parallel training runs
values.description: Several training runs are launched simultaneously to explore production-model parameters.

values.label: Sequential training runs
values.description: Training runs are launched one after another to explore suitable production-model parameters.

values.label: Deterministic reproducible training
values.description: Training is controlled so identical data and configuration produce reproducible models and results.

values.label: Direct DevOps operationalization
values.description: Conventional DevOps tools are applied without additional data, model, monitoring, or retraining capabilities.

clusters.name: Workflow Composition and Orchestration
clusters.description: Documents vary in how ML stages are modularized, connected, scheduled, and executed across interactive, automated, and distributed environments.

relations.rationale: An orchestrated workflow supplies the execution structure for deploying and invoking model-serving stages.
Workflow structure determines which lifecycle activities can be automated and monitored consistently.

values.label: Function-level workflow modularization
values.description: ML functionality is divided into reusable, versioned, documented functions that compose into larger workflows.

values.label: DSL-defined multi-stage graph

values.label: Kubeflow multi-stage composition
values.description: Reusable functions are composed into a Kubeflow pipeline covering preparation, training, and validation.

values.label: Interactive early-stage development

values.label: Uncoordinated pipeline recreation
values.description: Practitioners independently recreate equivalent workflow stages instead of sharing coordinated pipeline components.

clusters.name: ML Verification and Testing Strategy
clusters.description: Documents vary in how data, algorithms, pipelines, models, and production behavior are tested before and after release.

relations.rationale: Verification results determine whether a model or serving implementation is eligible for deployment.
Testing thresholds and validation outcomes restrict promotion and retraining decisions in production.

values.label: Held-out data evaluation
values.description: Models are evaluated on data not used during training to estimate generalization and deployment readiness.

values.label: Automated staged testing
values.description: Fast stateless unit tests precede broader integration, regression, and model-quality tests before deployment.

values.label: End-to-end pipeline integration testing

values.description: Training is deliberately interrupted to verify restoration from a saved checkpoint.

values.description: A model is loaded and exercised on real-life data in a canary stage before broad serving.

clusters.name: Model Serving Architecture

saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes through data preparation, training/search, orchestration, serving, deployment automation, testing, and production operations. However, several relevant architectural decisions are not fully subsumed. First, the deployment and operations dimensions do not explicitly model the hosting-topology decision between cloud, on-premises, and hybrid infrastructure, including retaining sensitive data on premises and managing the resulting boundary. Second, the taxonomy covers feature engineering and generic data storage but not the distinct feature-management decision of using an offline/online feature store, persisting prepared features, and replicating them for low-latency serving. Third, automated retraining is represented, but the alternative model-update strategy of continuous incremental learning from streams is not captured as a distinct training-lifecycle axis. Finally, model and data version repositories are covered, but experiment and training-run tracking/versioning—including parameters, datasets, metrics, and run provenance—is not explicitly represented and cannot be cleanly equated with artifact versioning.

uncovered_concepts: Online ingestion service as an enterprise data bus
Raw data storage with streaming pass-through
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes through workflow composition, execution infrastructure, serving, verification, deployment, monitoring, and feature transformation dimensions. However, it does not clearly capture the architectural decision of how ML software dependencies and runtime environments are declared, isolated, reproduced, and shared across training and production. This is distinct from infrastructure hosting (dimension 8) and artifact versioning (dimension 11). The minibatch also reveals a separate gap concerning data-ingestion and event-distribution architecture: whether ingestion is mediated by a decoupling data bus, how data is simultaneously persisted and streamed onward, and how events and data are distributed across computation regimes. Data storage organization captures physical persistence, but explicitly excludes retrieval and transformation, while data access responsibility captures ownership rather than ingestion topology. The remaining codes are subsumed by existing dimensions, especially workflow composition, training execution, model serving, release strategy, verification, monitoring, and data transformation.

uncovered_concepts: Machine-learning adoption despite an effective classical solution
Infrastructure, operations, project, and deployment activities
Agile architecture method for enterprise transformation
Lightweight process models for data science
saturation_history.rationale: Most codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: streaming, serverless, Spark, microservices, feature stores, distributed execution, serving, monitoring, verification, CI/CD, retraining, model registries, notebook use, responsibility allocation, and artifact tracking are all already represented. However, the taxonomy lacks a decision dimension for whether to adopt machine learning at all versus using a classical rule-based solution. It also does not explicitly capture event-schema and event-contract evolution, including serialization-format choice and tested migration procedures; ingestion and monitoring cover event flow and schema violations, but not the design of evolving event contracts or feature-store materialization from event streams. Finally, the minibatch exposes a distinct documentation and process-methodology axis: what lifecycle artifacts and decisions are documented, and whether teams use lightweight, CRISP-DM-based, agile, or more structured ML process methods. Existing reproducibility, workflow, and metadata dimensions capture tracking and execution, but not these documentation and process-method choices.

uncovered_concepts: Highly available eventually consistent feature storage
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: feature materialization and event sourcing fit Feature Management Strategy and Data Storage Organization; client/server, server-side, edge, batch, and API choices fit Model Packaging Strategy, Prediction Invocation and Routing, and ML Execution Infrastructure; notebook, IDE, container, dependency, and experimentation choices fit Experiment Reproducibility and Documentation and ML Execution Infrastructure; pipeline, CI/CD, registry, lineage, promotion, and rollout choices fit Deployment and Release Strategy; and monitoring, fairness, subgroup, business-impact, and human-review codes fit Production Monitoring Strategy, ML Verification Strategy, Remediation Trigger Strategy, and ML Governance and Access. However, highly available eventually consistent feature storage expresses a distinct feature-store consistency and availability trade-off. Existing dimensions cover where features are stored and how they are materialized, but do not capture the choice between consistency guarantees and availability/fault tolerance for feature-state storage without conflating separate architectural axes.

However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct axis for ML development technology and implementation style: the choice of programming language, framework/toolchain, editor, low-code versus conventional development, object-oriented versus notebook-oriented structure, and the strategy for reconciling development and production languages. These are practitioner-facing architectural choices driven by maintainability, available expertise, operational compatibility, and cost, and they cannot be cleanly absorbed into reproducibility, execution infrastructure, or model packaging without conflating different axes.

saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most ingestion, retention, integration, preparation, transformation, feature construction, representation, training-mode, experiment-reproducibility, and human-review codes. However, it lacks distinct dimensions for requirements and product-scope definition; iterative prototyping and user-feedback practices; CI and ML testing; prediction-serving and offline/nearline/online computation architecture; deployment and release orchestration; production observability and monitoring; model replacement and rollback policy; feature-computation serving mode; delivery/recovery measurement; and runtime infrastructure qualities such as scaling, failover, and automated recovery. Some related codes are covered indirectly—for example, offline versus online model training is covered by Model Training Execution, and data splitting is covered by Data Transformation Strategy—but these gaps cannot be absorbed without conflating separate architectural decision axes.

saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most minibatch codes, including feature and training-serving consistency, experiment tracking, CI/CD automation, model and data validation, monitoring and drift detection, retraining triggers, ordinary deployment packaging, and batch-versus-stream processing. However, several relevant architectural axes are not represented. First, deployment automation does not capture the serving target and runtime topology: cloud versus edge deployment, model-as-a-service, inference hardware, resource sizing, statelessness, or horizontal versus vertical scaling. Second, the taxonomy lacks an MLOps platform architecture dimension covering end-to-end managed platforms versus self-built, hybrid, or step-specific infrastructures, as well as microservice decomposition and replaceable providers or integrations. Third, it lacks an explicit objective-selection dimension for primary optimization goals and trade-offs such as accuracy versus speed or product engagement. Fourth, data governance concerns such as provenance, metadata cataloging, and privacy-preserving protection are not subsumed by ingestion, retention, cleaning, or integration. Fifth, production rollout and scoring-interaction strategies—shadow or multi-model rollout, traffic splitting, asynchronous score delivery, result persistence, and caching—are distinct from model evaluation and deployment automation. Finally, incremental-training-specific scaling and the choice between heuristic rules and a multivariable ML model are not clearly captured by the existing training-execution or model-selection dimensions.

saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most monitoring, preprocessing, training cadence, evaluation, deployment automation, serving-target, and workflow-orchestration codes. However, several relevant architectural decision axes are not represented. First, data-ingestion and data-storage architecture is missing: alternatives such as ordered acquisition/integration/ingestion pipelines, event streams versus raw data sources, transactional versus analytical access paths, repository technology choices, retention windows, and the resulting cold-start trade-offs cannot be absorbed by Data Preparation Implementation or Data Cleaning Strategy without conflating processing with source and storage architecture. Second, the model-building axis lacks explicit variation in model-family selection, hyperparameter-search strategy, and single-model versus ensemble construction. Third, production resilience lacks a distinct decision about serving a new model versus falling back to the previous model when latency or accuracy degrades; deployment automation mentions rollback but does not capture this runtime failure-policy axis. Fourth, feature acquisition and temporal correctness are not represented: retrieving features through chained service APIs, reconstructing historical feature state, and using scraping when point-in-time data is unavailable are distinct from feature encoding or preprocessing. Finally, model packaging and interchange-format selection—standalone generated code, PMML, PFA, ONNX, and coordinated management of model code and parameters—is not captured by deployment automation or serving target strategy.

Most codes are covered by existing dimensions: model families and AutoML by Model Selection Strategy; PMML, ONNX, persistence, and execution dependencies by Model Artifact Format; containers, deployment automation, profiling-related packaging, and live serving by Model Release Packaging and Serving Target Strategy; feature stores, online/offline features, event coordination, and storage choices by Feature Store Architecture, Data Storage Architecture, and Data Path Architecture; and pipeline, validation, retraining, CI/CD, and experiment execution by Pipeline Operation Strategy, Model Change Evaluation, and Build and Retraining Automation. First, ground-truth and label acquisition—including delayed labels and user-reported feedback—is distinct from the existing raw-data acquisition mechanisms. Second, MLOps platform sourcing is not represented: organizations may adopt an integrated managed suite or compose a custom ecosystem. Third, model-registry and lifecycle-management architecture is absent; artifact versioning does not subsume centralized publication, stage tracking, metadata, cross-environment registration, search, governance, and deletion protection. Fourth, production monitoring and observability is missing as a dimension covering telemetry collection, logging, alert thresholds, system and model-age metrics, predictive quality, bias, drift, and monitoring-triggered feedback. Finally, the choice between hybrid human-machine operation and fully automated operation is a distinct operational-autonomy decision, not merely a pipeline execution mode. Codes describing latency, performance gains, resource usage, accuracy, stakeholder engagement, transparency, and storage overhead are treated as forces or outcomes rather than additional dimensions.

uncovered_concepts: Microservice-oriented architecture for ML product integration
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: data acquisition, preparation, storage and paths cover ingestion, queues, analytical stores, processing modes, and query tooling; development packaging covers notebook-to-script transitions, testing, linting, and reuse; model selection and feature representation cover learner and feature-engineering choices; serving, artifact, release, monitoring, and MLOps dimensions cover container/serverless deployment, CI/CD, lifecycle monitoring, ownership, and operational concerns. However, the taxonomy does not explicitly capture the architectural decision of how ML functionality is decomposed and integrated as services within a product, including independent service boundaries, network-based interaction, and SLA contracts. It also lacks a distinct axis for runtime model-parameter state management: whether parameters are retrieved per request, persisted in a low-latency store, and updated atomically to prevent predictions from observing mixed versions. These are relevant architectural choices that cannot be absorbed into ordinary model artifact packaging, serving-target selection, or feature-store architecture without conflating distinct axes.

uncovered_concepts: NoSQL document database for raw data storage
ML metadata store for pipeline-run records
Synchronous feature queries with precomputed features
Programmatic policy-compliance checks across development and production
Server-side aggregation of device model updates
Local retention of personal training and testing data
saturation_history.rationale: The minibatch is not theoretically saturated. Many codes are covered by existing dimensions: ingestion timing and mechanisms, data preparation, build and validation, offline and online evaluation, release and registry, serving placement, capacity, monitoring, MLOps operating model, and retraining. However, several relevant architectural decision axes are absent. First, the taxonomy does not define a data-storage and persistence strategy; ingestion describes acquiring data but not immutable raw-data retention, database technology, or a unified data-access layer. Second, it lacks an explicit model-construction and optimization strategy covering automated model building, metric-driven search, feature selection, and hyperparameter tuning; offline evaluation alone does not subsume how candidate models are generated and optimized. Third, it lacks a pipeline-orchestration and run-provenance strategy for orchestrator control, pipeline metadata, intermediate-artifact tracking, and resumption. Fourth, it lacks a computation-mode strategy distinguishing offline, nearline, and online processing and their fallback trade-offs, as well as a distinct feature-computation strategy for asynchronous versus synchronous/precomputed features. Fifth, general ML-system decomposition into microservices versus a monolith is broader than the existing model-serving-form dimension. Finally, federated/on-device training, local data retention, and server-side update aggregation constitute a distinct distributed-training architecture not captured by serving placement or retraining; policy-compliance enforcement and model interpretability are also important lifecycle concerns without dedicated axes. Format-specific serialization, Git/CI workflows, edge deployment, monitoring variants, and ordinary model serving are otherwise absorbable by existing dimensions.

uncovered_concepts: Context-sensitive access control and information governance
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes concerning ingestion, preparation, orchestration triggers, endpoint serving, runtime placement, monitoring, validation, deployment automation, and operational cost or quality forces. However, several relevant architectural decisions are not subsumed by existing axes: the model algorithm or model-building approach; escalation of uncertain predictions to human reviewers; persistent data-storage strategy; access-control and information-governance architecture; packaging models as business-facing data products; decomposition granularity (for example, modular versus more consolidated architectures); and progressive or canary traffic rollout. In particular, deployment transition covers deployment, fallback, rollback, and performance-gated promotion, but not the distinct choice to increase production traffic gradually.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions, such as ingestion (1), repository choice (2), validation (6), packaging (7), release transition (20), and interface design (9). However, three overlaps remain: (1) Computation Timing Strategy (18) duplicates the timing and feature-computation choices in Inference Execution Strategy (10); rename 10 to focus on runtime placement and move values 10.4–10.6 to 18. (2) Data Preparation Architecture (3) overlaps Dataset Treatment Strategy (17), especially 3.6 and 17.2; move 3.6 to 17 and narrow 17 to dataset-level preprocessing/treatment, or otherwise assign those preprocessing values to only one dimension. (3) Data and Model Governance Strategy (14) overlaps MLOps Operating Model (15) through responsibility and ownership values 14.2–14.5 and 15.4; narrow 14 to access, governance, and compliance and move the operational responsibility choices to 15.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many decisions with generally understandable descriptions, such as computation timing (18), prediction interfaces (9), and production monitoring (11). However, several dimensions contain values that are difficult to distinguish. In Data Preparation Architecture (3), values 3.1 and 3.5 both describe integrated/reusable preparation pipelines, while 3.2 and 3.6 both describe generic preprocessing; merge the overlapping pairs or rename them to expose their concrete differences. In MLOps Operating Model (15), 15.1, 15.3, 15.5, and 15.7 substantially overlap around end-to-end, managed, or prebuilt platforms; merge redundant values and retain distinct platform/ownership alternatives. In Model Artifact Packaging Strategy (7), 7.1 is broad enough to overlap 7.3 and 7.4; rename 7.1 to clearly mean file-based packaging and reserve 7.4 for serialization formats. Value 20.1, Manual model deployment, is an actual decision alternative despite being marked outcome; reclassify it as a candidate status. Some descriptions, especially in 1 and 12, are terse and should be renamed or consolidated where overlapping labels such as scheduled/query-based ingestion and metadata-store/run-record tracking cannot be reliably separated.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: No material coverage shortcoming is evident under this criterion. The taxonomy represents the major workflow areas with decision dimensions having multiple candidates: ingestion (1), repositories (2), preparation and processing (3, 4, 17, 18), model construction and validation (19, 5, 6), packaging and provenance (7, 12), deployment and inference (20, 9, 10), and production operation and governance (11, 13, 14, 15). Even the smallest dimensions, Data Repository Strategy (2) and Dataset Treatment Strategy (17), contain several candidate decisions. Forces are not required because the specified format cannot express them.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy is broadly within scope: dimensions 1–13 and 17–20 cover ingestion, repositories, preparation, training automation, validation, packaging, release, serving, monitoring, and specialized deployment architectures. The main scope drift is dimension 14, “Data and Model Governance Strategy,” whose responsibility and accountability values (14.2–14.5) are organizational governance rather than architectural design decisions; retain only the access-control decision (14.1) or move these values into the operational dimension 15. Dimension 15, “MLOps Operating Model,” is partly relevant through platform choices (15.2, 15.3, 15.6, 15.7), but staffing and cost/time outcomes (15.4, 15.8, 15.9) are tangential to architectural decisions and should be moved to an existing operating/impact dimension or dropped.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No explicit catch-all dimensions or values appear. The taxonomy uses specific decision areas such as "Data Ingestion Strategy" (1), "Model Registry Strategy" (8), and "Production Monitoring Strategy" (11), with concrete alternatives rather than buckets named Other, Miscellaneous, General considerations, or Various techniques. No changes are needed for this criterion.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions do represent decisions, such as 1 Data Ingestion Strategy, 18 Computation Timing Strategy, and 20 Model Release Transition Strategy, but many dimensions combine multiple decision points while listing compatible practices rather than alternatives. Split 5 ML Integration Automation Strategy into CI adoption (5.1, 5.4, 5.5) and CI trigger choice (5.2, 5.3). Reorganize 6 Model Validation Strategy because values 6.1–6.9 are distinct test subtopics that can coexist, not options for one decision. Split 7 Model Artifact Packaging Strategy into packaging/dependency choices (7.1–7.3) and serialization/interoperability choices (7.4–7.5), preserving 7.5 as the outcome. Similarly, reorganize 12 ML Provenance Strategy and 14 Data and Model Governance Strategy, whose values describe separate lineage mechanisms and separate access, ownership, and accountability decisions rather than alternative answers to one question. Dimension 17 Dataset Treatment Strategy also combines augmentation and sanitization, which should not be treated as mutually exclusive alternatives.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many dimensions with multiple candidates, and outcome values are generally marked correctly, but numerous decision points combine different questions. For example, Data Ingestion Strategy (1) mixes transport mechanisms (1.1–1.5) with timing and collection approaches (1.6–1.8); split these into separate existing-content decision points. Data Repository Strategy (2) combines persistence, integration scope, and mutability (2.1–2.3), so separate those questions. Model Validation Strategy (6) mixes schema, feature, policy, model, and service testing; reorganize candidates into coherent validation questions, merging sibling test types where each group retains at least two candidates. Model Release Transition Strategy (20) combines deployment, fallback/rollback, traffic rollout, and promotion gating; split only into groups with at least two candidates or move values to the relevant existing decision points. Similar mixed-question problems occur in Prediction Interface Strategy (9), Inference Execution Strategy (10), Production Monitoring Strategy (11), Federated Learning Strategy (13), Governance (14), and MLOps Operating Model (15). No dimension has fewer than two candidate decisions, but the many broad, heterogeneous dimensions substantially reduce alignment with the required one-question-per-dimension structure.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy consistently uses accepted, rejected, mixed, and outcome statuses, and most descriptions match their status. The main violation is value 20.1, "Manual model deployment," in dimension 20 "Model Release Transition Strategy": it is phrased as an alternative deployment choice, not an effect, so it must be changed from status "outcome" to the appropriate candidate-decision status (accepted, rejected, or mixed). The other outcome values, such as 7.5, 15.8, and 15.9, are appropriately phrased as effects.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy places nearly all decision-bearing passages, including ingestion and immutable storage in dimensions 1–2 (s15_p03, s02_p03), AutoML and hyperparameter automation in dimension 19 (s19_p09, s17_p03, s18_p04), CI/CD and testing in dimensions 5–6 (s06_p14, s22_p12), packaging and reproducibility in dimensions 7 and 12 (s19_p09, s25_p02), and deployment, inference, and monitoring in dimensions 9–11 (s12_p07, s23_p10, s20_p03). Two passages cannot be placed: s13_p07 discusses choosing process methodologies such as ASUM-DM versus the IBM Cloud Garage/agile method and cultural change; add a process-methodology value to dimension 15, MLOps Operating Model, or add a dedicated process-strategy dimension. s10_p02 discusses product safeguards, anomaly detection, and choosing heuristics versus machine learning for fraud mitigation; add a risk-detection strategy dimension with values for product controls, anomaly detection, heuristics, and ML.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage

criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many explicit choices, including ingestion patterns from s15_p03 and s02_p03, online and incremental updating from s19_p09 and s20_p03, AutoML model selection and HPO from s19_p09 and s17_p03, CI/testing from s06_p14 and s22_p12, and microservice/monolith alternatives from s07_p03 and s16_p07. Missing options remain: add values such as serverless deployment to dimension 17 (s07_p03); add infrastructure-compatibility, prediction-API, load/performance, data-validation, and predictive-target release tests to dimension 12 (s06_p14); add product verification changes and anomaly detection to an appropriate risk/model-strategy dimension (s10_p02); add NoSQL document storage and immutable raw-data retention to the data-storage/ingestion dimensions (s02_p03), and add model auditability/team collaboration to dimension 16 or a new monitoring dimension (s23_p10).

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions ask distinct questions, such as data acquisition (1), storage (22), and serving target (17), but important overlaps remain. Move value 11.5 "Automated feature engineering" from Model Selection Strategy (11) to Feature Representation Strategy (7) or Data Preparation Implementation (2), since it answers a preparation/representation question rather than model selection. Move 13.6 "Previous-model fallback" and 13.7 "Previous-model rollback" to Model Release Packaging (15), where deployment transition and rollback belong. Separate the packaging question in 15 from artifact serialization in Model Artifact Format (20), moving packaging-oriented value 20.1 to 15 while retaining formats such as PMML, PFA, and ONNX in 20. Clarify the overlap between 15.2 "Pipeline-based web-service deployment" and 17.2 "Web-service model deployment" by keeping the value answering release packaging in 15 and the value answering serving target in 17. Feature-result repository values in Data Storage Architecture (22.5-22.8) also substantially overlap Feature Store Architecture (24) and should be moved to the dimension whose question they answer. These overlaps are significant for a taxonomy intended to represent one ML architectural decision per dimension.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy usually provides recognizable names, descriptions, candidate statuses, and outcome statuses, but several dimensions have overlapping values or ranges that do not match their names. In dimension 1, messaging-queue, event-based, trigger-based publish-subscribe, and scheduled ingestion are not clearly separated as mechanism versus timing choices; split or reorganize these alternatives around those questions. In dimension 2, values 2.1, 2.3, and 2.5 are near-synonyms for reusable transformation implementation, while 2.7 and 2.8 both describe preparation outputs; reorganize them into clearly distinct implementation and output alternatives. Dimension 15 is broader than model packaging because values 15.1, 15.2, and 15.6 describe deployment and rollback, and 15.1 is labeled as an outcome despite being a candidate decision; rename or reorganize the dimension and classify that value consistently. Dimension 17 has overlapping real-time endpoint and web-service values (17.1 and 17.2), while 17.7 is a scaling choice rather than a serving target; merge the overlapping values and remove or relocate the scaling value. In dimension 20, 20.5 describes client integration rather than an artifact format; move it to the deployment/serving dimension.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers most workflow areas with multiple candidates, including ingestion (1.1–1.9), preparation (2.1–2.10), orchestration (3.3–3.10), model selection (11.1–11.9), release (15.1–15.6), serving (17.1–17.7), storage (22.1–22.8), and feature stores (24.1–24.9). A major gap is production operation and observability: dimension 13, "Model Change Evaluation," focuses on validation and rollback, while dimension 14, "Build and Retraining Automation," focuses on triggers, so there is no clear decision point for alternative monitoring/alerting strategies. Reframe dimension 13 as a production evaluation and monitoring strategy and move monitoring-related trigger values such as 14.8 and 14.9 into it, while retaining the remaining build and retraining candidates in dimension 14. Training architecture is also only indirectly represented through dimension 11 and should be made more explicit by reorganizing its existing model-selection and automation values around distinct training choices rather than leaving training embedded in selection.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Nearly all dimensions map directly to the stated ML workflow, including ingestion (1), preparation and orchestration (2–3), feature and model decisions (7, 11, 13), automation and deployment (14–20), and data/feature platform architecture (22–24). Dimension 25, "ML Project Framing," is mainly project methodology and business-process guidance: values such as 25.3 Iterative lean delivery, 25.4 CRISP-DM process model, and 25.6 Unrestricted framework choice are outside architectural decisions practitioners make during ingestion, processing, training, production, and operations. Drop dimension 25 and its values; the remaining dimensions are substantially in scope.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No dimension or value is a catch-all bucket. Across the ML workflow—from Data Acquisition Strategy and Data Preparation Implementation through Model Release Packaging, Serving Target Strategy, and Feature Store Architecture—the taxonomy uses concrete alternatives such as messaging-queue ingestion, holdout evaluation, containerized deployment, and centralized feature store. It contains no values or dimensions named Other, Miscellaneous, General considerations, or equivalent broad buckets, so no reorganization is needed for this criterion.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The output uses the required JSON structure and often presents plausible alternatives, but many dimensions combine multiple independent decisions, contrary to the requirement that each dimension name one architectural design decision. Dimension 3, "Pipeline Operation Strategy," mixes execution parity, manuality, orchestration, scheduling, and notebook-to-project transition; split it into separate execution/orchestration and development-to-production decisions. Dimension 11, "Model Selection Strategy," combines model-family choice, hyperparameter tuning, ensembles, optimization metrics, feature engineering, and fraud approaches; reorganize these into distinct existing decision topics and move value 11.5 to feature representation/preparation. Dimension 14, "Build and Retraining Automation," combines CI, change triggers, retraining triggers, and artifact versioning; split automation/versioning from retraining-trigger choice. Dimension 15, "Model Release Packaging," combines artifact packaging with deployment and rollback strategy; separate those values into packaging versus release-promotion decisions. Dimension 22, "Data Storage Architecture," combines storage medium, database family, and repository role; split it into storage technology and storage-role decisions. Similar bundling also occurs in 24, "Feature Store Architecture," and 25, "ML Project Framing," but the listed issues are the most substantial.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many candidate values, but numerous dimensions answer several different decision questions. Most notably, 3 Pipeline Operation Strategy mixes parity, manual operation, orchestration, scheduling, notebook use, project structure, and anomaly halting; split it into the parity, manual-versus-automated operation, and notebook-to-project decisions, while moving singleton topics to matching existing decision points. Similarly, 11 Model Selection Strategy mixes model-family choice, hyperparameter tuning, feature engineering, optimization metrics, and fraud heuristics; move 11.5 to 7 Feature Representation Strategy and keep the tuning alternatives together. Dimension 7 mixes encoding, feature engineering, schema representation, and point-in-time correctness; split the encoding values 7.1-7.3 from transformation values 7.4-7.5, and move 7.6 and 7.7 to decision points answering their respective questions. Dimension 14 mixes CI/CD, retraining, retraining triggers, and artifact versioning; separate the trigger alternatives 14.5-14.9 and move versioning 14.10 to the artifact-management decision. Dimension 13 mixes evaluation methods with fallback and rollback responses; keep 13.1-13.5 as evaluation alternatives and move 13.6-13.7 to release/deployment handling. Other broad dimensions such as 15, 17, 22, 23, 24, and 25 have the same structural problem, so despite generally having at least two values, the overall alignment with one-question-per-dimension is weak.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Most values use valid statuses, and the outcome values in dimensions 13, 20, and 24 are generally described as effects rather than alternatives. However, dimension 15 value 15.1 "Manual model deployment" is marked as an outcome even though its label and description present a deployment option; reclassify it as an accepted or rejected candidate decision, or rewrite it as an actual deployment consequence. The rejected values 2.10 "Notebook-based large-scale experimentation" and 11.9 "Boxed AutoML tool" are described affirmatively as practices that are performed or used, which conflicts with their rejected status; revise those descriptions to explicitly indicate non-adoption or change their statuses to match the descriptions.

criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers many adopted options, including ingestion modes in s15_p03 and s02_p03, AutoML and hyperparameter automation in s19_p09, s17_p03, and s18_p04, CI/CD and validation practices in s06_p14, serialization in s19_p09, and online/offline computation and monitoring in s12_p07 and s23_p10. Missing options include: add 'ASUM-DM process model' and 'IBM Cloud Garage Method' to dimension 15, MLOps Operating Model, supported by s13_p07; add 'relational SQL repository', 'distributed NoSQL/key-value repository', and a hybrid offline-plus-online computation option to dimensions 2, Data Repository Strategy, and 18, Computation Timing Strategy, supported by s12_p07; add 'mixed or hybrid architecture' to dimension 9, Prediction Interface Strategy, supported by s16_p07; add a Fraud Mitigation Strategy dimension with 'product changes', 'anomaly detection', and 'heuristic or ML detection', supported by s10_p02; and add 'automated repeated test execution' to dimension 6, Model Validation Strategy, supported by s22_p12.
